content.title: About
content.content: Barbecue beef with sauce is made from selected cuts of beef marinated in aromatic spices and a sweet‑tangy tomato‑based sauce, then slowly baked until tender. The product is ready to eat: simply heat and serve as a main dish or use in salads, sandwiches, and pastas.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The classic barbecue recipe originates from the southern United States, where meat was traditionally cooked over open fire.
The sauce combines tomato paste, brown sugar, vinegar, and smoky spices, giving it a distinctive sweet‑sour flavor.
The beef used is typically from the rib or chuck, cuts rich in connective tissue that become especially juicy after long simmering.
When stored properly in the refrigerator, the product retains its flavor for up to 7 days.
Some versions add a dash of liquid smoke to enhance the smoky aroma.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Beef provides all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Iron and zinc
items.content: Red meat is a good source of heme iron and zinc, supporting immune function and metabolism.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, important for the nervous system and energy production.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: The product fits low‑carb diets as it contains virtually no sugar.

items.title: Antioxidant content
items.content: Spices and tomato sauce provide antioxidants that help protect cells.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The sauce can be salty; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Beef contains saturated fats, so moderate consumption is advised for heart‑related conditions.

items.title: Heat treatment
items.content: The product must be heated to an internal temperature of 75 °C to eliminate food‑borne risks.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the product in a microwave or skillet until hot. Serve with vegetables, mashed potatoes, or use as a filling for burgers and tacos. Fresh herbs or a squeeze of lime can brighten the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C in the original packaging or an airtight container. Once opened, keep for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C; fully thaw and reheat before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: The Chicken Fillet Biscuit is a fast‑food item consisting of a tender chicken fillet baked inside a crisp biscuit‑style coating. Served hot, it is often accompanied by a sauce and a side.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The biscuit coating makes the dish lighter than traditional deep‑fried breading.
In some restaurants the fillet is marinated in spices and yogurt before coating for extra juiciness.
The biscuit batter is made from eggs, flour, milk, and a small amount of leavening, giving it an airy texture.
The portion is usually sized for quick, on‑the‑go consumption.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken fillet provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Lower fat content
items.content: Compared with fried breaded options, the biscuit coating contains less saturated fat.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken supplies vitamin B6 and niacin, which support metabolic processes.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: The dish provides phosphorus and selenium, important for bone health and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Salt is often added to the coating for flavor; people monitoring sodium intake should limit portions.

items.title: Cooking safety
items.content: Undercooked fillet can harbor harmful bacteria; ensure the internal temperature reaches 75 °C (165 °F).

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The Chicken Fillet Biscuit is convenient to eat with your hands as a quick snack, or you can slice it and serve with sauce, salad, or mashed potatoes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared product in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight container for up to 1 month. Reheat until the internal temperature reaches 75 °C.

egg-whole-fried-with-animal-fat-or-meat-.title: Egg, whole, fried with animal fat or meat drippings

content.title: About
content.content: Eggs are a nutrient‑dense food produced by chickens. When fried in animal fat or meat drippings they acquire a distinctive flavor and a higher calorie count compared with cooking without added fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Frying eggs in animal fat is a traditional technique in many cuisines, including French, Spanish and American home cooking.
The type of fat used influences taste and texture: butter yields a softer egg, while lard creates a crispier edge.
Eggs cooked in animal fat retain most of their B‑vitamins and minerals, but they also contain more saturated fat.
In 1933 this method was common in households because lard and butter were readily available.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A large egg provides about 6 g of complete protein, essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin D
items.content: The yolk is one of the few natural food sources of vitamin D, important for bone health and immune function.

items.title: Contains choline
items.content: Choline supports liver function and brain health, aiding memory and concentration.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Eggs supply iron, zinc and selenium, which play roles in metabolism and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Supports eye health
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin in the yolk help protect the eyes from age‑related degeneration.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Frying in animal fat adds saturated fat, which can raise cholesterol levels if consumed frequently.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Eggs fried in fat are more calorie‑dense, which should be considered in weight‑management plans.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked eggs may contain Salmonella; cook until the yolk is fully set to reduce risk.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Egg white protein is a common allergen, especially in children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fried eggs are served hot, often seasoned with salt and pepper. They can be placed in sandwiches, salads, burgers, or enjoyed on their own as a classic breakfast.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw eggs in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C in their original carton. Cooked fried eggs should be eaten within 2 hours at room temperature or refrigerated and consumed within 24 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Grilled catfish fillet is a tender piece of freshwater fish with a light smoky flavor. Catfish, native to rivers and lakes, is known for its firm, mildly sweet flesh. Grilling preserves its nutrients while giving the surface a crisp, caramelized crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Catfish can grow over a meter long and weigh more than 20 kg, but culinary preparations usually use smaller fillets.
The meat is rich in protein and omega‑3 fatty acids, which are heart‑healthy.
Traditionally, catfish is grilled over open fire in Southeast Asian cuisines, often marinated in soy sauce and spices.
Grilling helps retain the fish’s natural taste, reducing the need for strong seasonings.
Catfish is sometimes called the “king of freshwater fish” because of its flavor profile.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Catfish fillet provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of omega‑3
items.content: Omega‑3 fatty acids support cardiovascular health and reduce inflammation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides selenium, phosphorus, and potassium, important for thyroid function and electrolyte balance.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many meat products, catfish has moderate fat content, making it suitable for balanced diets.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including catfish.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Freshwater fish can accumulate mercury and other toxins; moderate consumption is advised.

items.title: Overconsumption
items.content: Large portions may lead to excess protein and calories.

items.title: Parasite risk
items.content: Undercooked or raw pieces may contain parasites; ensure the fish is fully cooked.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the grilled catfish fillet hot, often with lemon, fresh herbs, or a light yogurt‑based sauce. It can be added to salads, rice or vegetable dishes, and used in sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked fillet in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 63 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Steak sandwich on white bread (1731) is a hearty sandwich featuring thinly sliced, grilled steak placed between two slices of soft white bread. It is often complemented with lettuce, tomato, onion, and sauces such as mustard or mayo.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish is popular in American diners and is commonly served as a quick lunch.
White bread provides a soft texture that lets the flavor of the meat shine.
Traditionally the steak is cooked to medium doneness to retain juiciness.
The sandwich can be customized with cheese, bacon, or avocado.
Some eateries use seeded bread for added crunch.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Steak is an excellent source of high‑quality protein, essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Red meat provides heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Steak supplies B12, B6, and niacin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Moderate healthy fats
items.content: When lean cuts (e.g., sirloin) are used, the sandwich includes beneficial monounsaturated fats.

items.title: Provides fiber from bread and veggies
items.content: White bread and added vegetables contribute a modest amount of dietary fiber for digestion.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: White bread contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Sauces and processed ingredients can raise the salt level, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Using fatty cuts or adding cheese can increase saturated fat intake.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked steak may harbor harmful bacteria; it should be cooked to a safe internal temperature.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the sandwich hot, cut in half. It can be eaten by hand or with a fork and knife. Add fresh vegetables, mustard, or a light mayo to enhance flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared sandwich in the refrigerator, wrapped in plastic, for up to 24 hours. Bread may become dry, so reheat in an oven or toaster before serving.
